title: When One Agent Is Not Enough

questions.question: An agent keeps choosing the wrong one of several similar tools. What should you try before splitting it into several agents?
options: Add a second agent to check it
Improve tool names and descriptions, or select fewer tools per task
questions.explanation: Most tool-choice errors are description problems, which splitting doesn't fix.

questions.question: With vague domain descriptions, the router design scored worse than one agent. Why?
options: Requests routed to the wrong specialist can't be recovered; the router added its own errors
questions.explanation: Overall accuracy is roughly router accuracy times specialist accuracy.

questions.question: Why did three workers read fewer tokens in total than one agent doing all three research threads?
options: Each model call re-reads its context; workers never re-read the other threads' results
questions.explanation: In one window, every later call pays for every earlier result.

questions.question: A task has one long thread whose context exceeds the window, with no independent parts. What's the better fix?
options: Compress or summarise the context within one agent
questions.explanation: Splitting needs separable work; otherwise you just add handoffs.

questions.question: Which pressure justifies separate agents even when tools and context are small?
options: Parts that need different trust levels, like reading untrusted email and sending payments
questions.explanation: Isolation keeps untrusted input from steering dangerous tools.

questions.question: Anthropic reported its multi-agent research system used about 15 times the tokens of a chat. What does that suggest about the toy's 71,600 vs 166,600 result?
options: Splitting saves tokens per unit of work, but teams usually do more work, so total cost often rises
questions.explanation: Budget for the extra work, not just the per-call savings.
